traditions.name: Virtue Ethics
traditions.description: The good life and moral character — from ancient eudaimonia to modern virtue theory, asking what it means to live well and act excellently

traditions.name: Deontology
traditions.description: Duty, rights, and the moral law — grounding ethics in rational principles that bind regardless of consequences

traditions.name: Consequentialism
traditions.description: Outcomes, welfare, and the greater good — the view that the moral worth of actions is determined by their consequences

traditions.name: Social Contract & Political Philosophy
traditions.description: Agreement, justice, and political legitimacy — deriving moral and political obligations from rational agreement or rights

traditions.name: Metaethics
traditions.description: The nature and status of moral claims — whether moral judgments are objective, what moral language means, and how values relate to the natural world

traditions.name: Moral Psychology
traditions.description: Agency, motivation, and moral experience — how moral agents think, choose, and bear responsibility for their actions

traditions.name: Applied & Normative Ethics
traditions.description: Ethics in practice — bringing moral theory to bear on concrete problems through case reasoning and thought experiments

philosophers.name: Plato
philosophers.core_assumptions: Justice is not a mere social convention or instrument of power but a real structural feature of the soul, analogous to health in the body. The soul has distinct parts with distinct functions, and virtue consists in each part performing its proper role under the governance of reason. A well-ordered city mirrors the well-ordered soul, so political philosophy and moral psychology are inseparable inquiries.
signature_moves: Using the city-soul analogy to make the structure of justice visible at a larger scale before turning inward
Employing elenctic refutation to demolish interlocutors' definitions before constructing his own positive account
Arguing from function (ergon) to virtue: whatever has a function has a corresponding excellence

signature_attack.name: Form of the Good
signature_attack.description: Forces player to define the highest good

philosophers.thinking_text: Plato gazes toward the realm of Forms...
philosophers.defeat_text: The shadows on the cave wall flicker and reform. Perhaps there is more to justice than I had shown you -- you have glimpsed something beyond the Forms themselves.
philosophers.victory_text: Return to the cave and consider again. The Form of the Good does not reveal itself to those who look away.

opening_statements.text:
Let me lay out my argument plainly, so you can see where you must attack it if you can. First premise: everything that has a function has a corresponding excellence — a knife cuts well, an eye sees well, and each is good precisely insofar as it performs its proper work. Second premise: the soul has a function — it deliberates, governs, and directs a life. Therefore the soul has a corresponding excellence, and we call that excellence justice.

Now, Thrasymachus claims justice is merely the advantage of the stronger — a convention imposed by the powerful. But consider: if a tyrant's soul is disordered, with appetite ruling over reason, then by what right does he call his advantage 'justice'? He cannot even govern himself. His soul is like a body wracked by disease, each organ at war with the others.

The just soul, by contrast, achieves internal harmony — reason commanding, spirit enforcing, appetite obeying — and this harmony is not a convention any more than health is a convention. You do not vote on whether a diseased body is healthy.

Therefore justice is an objective structural feature of the soul, and the just person is necessarily happier than the unjust, regardless of reputation, wealth, or worldly success. I defy you to show me otherwise.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider a disciplined, calculating tyrant whose reason fully governs spirit and appetite — yet reason directs him to enslave others for personal gain. His soul has the exact structural harmony you describe, but he is manifestly unjust. Your argument conflates internal order with moral goodness.
move_hints.reductio: If injustice is literally disease of the soul — analogous to illness in the body — then unjust people are sick, not wicked. But then punishment makes no sense; we should offer therapy, not retribution. Your analogy eliminates moral responsibility entirely.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You argue from function to excellence: the soul's function is to govern, so its excellence is governing well. But how do you determine what counts as 'governing well' without already knowing what justice is? Does your argument reason in a circle?
move_hints.framework_shift: A Humean would reject the hidden premise of your entire argument — that the soul has a natural hierarchy with reason on top. If reason is merely the servant of the passions, there is no 'proper order' for justice to consist in, and your function argument has no foundation.

opening_statements.text:
I will now demonstrate that most people are morally ignorant, and that this follows necessarily from the nature of knowledge itself. Here is my argument.

First: genuine knowledge requires grasping objects that are stable, unchanging, and fully real — the Forms. Opinion, by contrast, latches onto the shifting world of particulars, which are always becoming but never simply are. Second: moral knowledge — knowing what justice, courage, or goodness truly is — requires grasping the Form of Justice, the Form of Courage, the Form of the Good. These cannot be apprehended through the senses.

Third: most people never turn their minds from the sensible world toward the intelligible world. They live, as it were, chained in a cave, watching shadows cast by firelight on the wall, and they mistake these flickering images for the whole of reality. They argue about the shadows — which comes first, which is largest — never suspecting that the true objects are behind them, and the sun above.

Therefore most people have opinion about moral matters, not knowledge. They may happen upon correct moral judgments the way a blind person may happen upon the right road, but they cannot give an account of why it is right, and their correctness is unstable.

Only the philosopher who ascends from the cave — who grasps the Form of the Good that illuminates all other Forms as the sun illuminates visible things — possesses genuine moral knowledge. Everyone else is guessing.

move_hints.counterexample: An experienced parent or community elder with no philosophical training often displays deep moral wisdom — knowing when to be merciful, when to be firm, how to navigate conflicting obligations. If moral knowledge requires grasping the Forms, how do you explain the moral competence of people who have never contemplated a single Form?
move_hints.reductio: If only philosophers who grasp the Form of the Good possess genuine moral knowledge, then the vast majority of humankind is morally blind. But you also claim the just person is happiest. It follows that almost no one is capable of genuine happiness — your theory condemns humanity to permanent moral and eudaimonic failure.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say the Form of the Good illuminates all other Forms as the sun illuminates visible things. But can you describe the Good itself — not its effects, but its nature? If you cannot say what the Good is, only what it does, how can it serve as the foundation of all moral knowledge?
move_hints.framework_shift: Aristotle argues that practical wisdom is developed through experience and habituation in particular situations, not through contemplation of abstract, separated Forms. Ethics is a practical science whose precision matches its subject matter — and its subject matter is the variable world of human action, not an unchanging realm of being.

philosophers.name: Aristotle
philosophers.core_assumptions: Ethics is not a theoretical science but a practical one: its purpose is not merely to know what virtue is but to become virtuous. Human beings have a characteristic function (ergon), and the good life consists in performing that function excellently over a complete life. Precision must be calibrated to subject matter -- ethics admits of generalizations that hold only for the most part, and a well-brought-up person's moral perceptions are themselves a form of evidence.
signature_moves: Beginning from reputable opinions (endoxa) and ordinary usage, then refining them through careful distinction rather than rejecting them wholesale
Locating virtue as a mean between two vices -- one of excess, one of deficiency -- relative to the agent and situation
Using the function argument to ground the human good in the excellent exercise of the soul's rational capacities

signature_attack.name: Golden Mean
signature_attack.description: Exposes the excess or deficiency in the player's position

philosophers.thinking_text: Aristotle surveys the situation with practical wisdom...
philosophers.defeat_text: A well-aimed argument, delivered with the practical wisdom of experience. The virtuous person learns from being bested.
philosophers.victory_text: Virtue is a mean, and you have missed it. Go practice -- ethics is learned by doing, not by arguing badly.

philosophers.name: Thomas Hobbes
philosophers.core_assumptions: Human beings are fundamentally equal in their capacity to kill one another, and in the absence of a common power to keep them in awe, this equality produces a war of all against all. There is no natural moral order prior to the sovereign's commands -- right and wrong, justice and injustice, have no place without enforceable law. Reason is purely instrumental: it calculates the means to self-preservation, and the laws of nature are theorems about how to achieve peace.
signature_moves: Deriving moral and political obligation from a hypothetical state of nature designed to terrify the reader into accepting sovereignty
Defining key normative terms reductively -- justice as covenant-keeping, right as liberty, law as constraint -- to eliminate any appeal to an independent moral order
Using the logic of strategic interaction: showing that without enforcement, rational agents will defect even when cooperation would benefit all

signature_attack.name: State of Nature
signature_attack.description: Strips away civilization to reveal the war of all against all

philosophers.thinking_text: Hobbes calculates the balance of power...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have found order without my Leviathan. I concede the field -- but watch for the war that follows.
philosophers.victory_text: Without a sovereign argument, your position is the war of all against all. Submit or perish.

philosophers.name: David Hume
philosophers.core_assumptions: All ideas are derived from impressions of sense or reflection, and any concept that cannot be traced to such an impression is suspect. Moral distinctions are not discovered by reason alone -- reason can establish relations of ideas and matters of fact, but neither of these operations yields a moral judgment. Morality is fundamentally a matter of sentiment: we feel approval and disapproval, and these feelings constitute our moral awareness.
signature_moves: Challenging rationalism by showing that reason alone cannot motivate action -- it requires a prior desire or sentiment to set ends
Deploying the is-ought gap: noting that writers imperceptibly shift from 'is' and 'is not' to 'ought' and 'ought not' without explaining the transition
Using counterexamples that strip away every rational candidate for the source of moral judgment, leaving only sentiment standing
key_works: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals

signature_attack.name: Is-Ought Guillotine
signature_attack.description: Severs the player's attempt to derive values from facts

philosophers.thinking_text: Hume raises a skeptical eyebrow and consults his sentiments...
philosophers.defeat_text: My sentiments approve of your reasoning, even as my philosophy insists they shouldn't. Well played.
philosophers.victory_text: Reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions -- and your passions have led you astray.

philosophers.name: Immanuel Kant
philosophers.core_assumptions: Morality cannot be grounded in empirical facts about human nature, inclination, or consequences -- it must be derived from pure practical reason alone. A genuinely moral law must be universal and necessary, binding on all rational beings as such. The will is autonomous: it legislates the moral law for itself, and this self-legislation is the source of human dignity and the foundation of all moral worth.
signature_moves: Isolating the concept of duty through increasingly extreme thought experiments that strip away every empirical motive until only the pure motive of duty remains
Formulating the same moral law in multiple ways -- universal law, humanity as end, kingdom of ends -- to reveal different aspects of a single rational principle
Drawing sharp architectonic distinctions: hypothetical vs. categorical imperatives, legality vs. morality, autonomy vs. heteronomy
key_works: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals

signature_attack.name: Categorical Imperative
signature_attack.description: Forces universalizability test on player's position

philosophers.thinking_text: Kant formulates a maxim...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have found a maxim I cannot universalize against. Duty compels me to acknowledge your victory.
philosophers.victory_text: Your maxim cannot be universalized. You have treated yourself as an exception, which is the root of all moral failure.

opening_statements.text:
I ask you to follow this argument to its conclusion, and then to show me where, if anywhere, the reasoning fails. Nothing in the world — or beyond it — can be called good without qualification except a good will.

Why? Because every other candidate for the good is conditional: intelligence serves the clever criminal, courage steadies the resolute tyrant, and even happiness corrupts if it inflates the pride of someone unworthy of it. Only a good will is good in itself, not as a means to something else.

Now, what makes a will good? Not its consequences — for consequences depend on fortune, and the moral worth of a person cannot be hostage to luck. A will is good when it acts from duty, that is, from respect for the moral law itself.

And what is the moral law? It cannot be any particular command drawn from experience, because experience tells us only what is, never what ought to be, and moral necessity is universal — binding on every rational being in every circumstance. Therefore the moral law must be purely formal: act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.

This is the categorical imperative. It is not my invention — it is the principle your own reason legislates the moment you think morally at all. Deny it, and you deny the very rationality that makes argument possible.

move_hints.counterexample: A person who tells the truth to a murderer asking where his victim is hiding acts from a universalizable maxim — 'always tell the truth' — yet produces a monstrous outcome. A person who lies to save the victim acts from a maxim that fails universalization, yet acts rightly. Your theory systematically misidentifies moral worth in cases where duty and decency diverge.
move_hints.reductio: If moral worth lies solely in the motive of duty, then two people performing identical acts of kindness differ in moral worth based on whether one acts from affection and the other from cold obligation. Taken seriously, your view implies that the person who helps others only because duty compels her — feeling nothing — is morally superior to the person who helps from genuine love. That is a perverse moral psychology.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say we must act only on universalizable maxims. But any action can be described under many maxims — 'lie to save a life,' 'lie when convenient,' 'protect the innocent.' Different descriptions yield different verdicts. How do you determine which maxim is the correct one to test, without smuggling in a prior moral judgment about what matters?
move_hints.framework_shift: From the standpoint of virtue ethics, your architecture severs morality from the emotions, relationships, and particularities that give it meaning. A moral theory in which compassion, love, and loyalty have zero moral worth — because they are inclinations rather than duties — has amputated the heart of ethical life.

opening_statements.text:
I will now demonstrate that every rational being must be treated as an end in itself, never merely as a means. Follow the argument.

First premise: a rational being possesses autonomy — the capacity to set its own ends through reason, rather than being determined by natural impulse. Second premise: autonomy is the ground of dignity, and dignity differs fundamentally from price. Whatever has a price can be exchanged for something of equivalent value; whatever has dignity is elevated above all price and permits no equivalent.

Third premise: the capacity for rational self-legislation — for binding oneself to universal moral principles through one's own reason — is unique among all capacities in nature. Nothing else in the natural world gives itself laws. It follows that rational nature exists as an end in itself. This is not a sentimental claim about human specialness — it is a structural fact about what rationality is.

When you treat a rational being merely as a tool for your own purposes, you contradict the very principle that makes morality possible, for you deny in practice the autonomy that you presuppose in yourself whenever you deliberate about what to do.

Therefore: act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end and never merely as a means. This is not a separate imperative — it is the same categorical imperative viewed from the standpoint of the rational beings it governs.

move_hints.counterexample: Infants, persons with severe cognitive disabilities, and individuals in permanent vegetative states all lack the rational autonomy you describe, yet they clearly possess moral standing — perhaps even heightened claims on our protection. If dignity depends on rational self-legislation, your theory excludes precisely those who most need moral consideration.
move_hints.reductio: If treating someone merely as a means violates their autonomy, then every market transaction — paying a cashier, hailing a taxi, hiring a plumber — risks moral violation. You add 'merely' to avoid this, but follow the logic: an employer who pays fair wages, provides benefits, and observes labor laws, yet internally views workers as nothing but production inputs, treats them merely as means in his will even if not in his actions. Your criterion turns on inner attitudes we can never verify.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say autonomy — rational self-legislation — is the ground of all dignity. But what gives autonomy itself its special status? If you say 'reason values autonomy,' then reason is doing the grounding, not autonomy. If you say autonomy is self-grounding — valuable because it values itself — is that not viciously circular?
move_hints.framework_shift: Care ethics begins from the observation that we are not isolated rational legislators but fundamentally dependent beings embedded in relationships of care, vulnerability, and mutual need. Your dignity framework cannot account for the moral significance of dependence, embodiment, and emotional connection — the very things that make ethics urgent.

philosophers.name: Jeremy Bentham
philosophers.core_assumptions: Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters -- pleasure and pain -- and any moral theory that denies this is fighting against reality rather than reasoning about it. The principle of utility, which approves of every action according to its tendency to augment or diminish happiness, is the only defensible foundation for morals and legislation. Pleasures and pains are measurable along determinate dimensions, and moral reasoning is ultimately a species of calculation.
signature_moves: Deflating rival moral principles by showing they either reduce to utility in disguise or amount to mere expressions of personal sentiment
Operationalizing moral judgment through the felicific calculus: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, extent
Treating moral vocabulary with suspicion -- exposing 'ought' claims as either covert appeals to pleasure and pain or meaningless noise
key_works: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

signature_attack.name: Felicific Calculus
signature_attack.description: Reduces the player's position to a cold calculation of pleasure and pain

philosophers.thinking_text: Bentham tallies pleasures and pains on his felicific calculus...
philosophers.defeat_text: The calculus does not lie -- the balance of argument favors you. I shall record this outcome for future legislative reference.
philosophers.victory_text: The calculus is clear: your position produces more pain than pleasure. Back to the drawing board.

philosophers.name: John Stuart Mill
philosophers.core_assumptions: The utilitarian standard is not the agent's own greatest happiness but the greatest amount of happiness altogether -- utilitarianism demands impartiality. Pleasures differ in quality as well as quantity, and the verdict of competent judges who have experienced both higher and lower pleasures settles the question of which is more desirable. The proof of the principle of utility cannot be deductive but proceeds by showing that happiness is the only thing people actually desire as an end.
signature_moves: Defending utilitarianism by reinterpreting rather than abandoning common moral intuitions -- showing that justice, rights, and virtue all find their proper foundation in utility
Introducing qualitative distinctions among pleasures to answer the 'swine objection' while remaining within a broadly hedonistic framework
Appealing to the competent judge: someone who has experienced both kinds of pleasure is the only authority on which is preferable

signature_attack.name: Higher Pleasures
signature_attack.description: Challenges the player to distinguish quality from quantity of happiness

philosophers.thinking_text: Mill weighs the quality of the pleasures at stake...
philosophers.defeat_text: A competent judge would rank your argument among the higher pleasures. I yield with admiration.
philosophers.victory_text: A competent judge would not prefer your argument. You have mistaken a lower pleasure for a higher one.

philosophers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral values are not timeless truths but historical products with genealogies that reveal their origins in power, resentment, and social struggle. The dominant moral framework of Western civilization -- which privileges humility, pity, and self-denial -- was not discovered by reason but invented by the weak as a weapon against the strong. Understanding the origin of moral concepts requires a new kind of inquiry: genealogy, which replaces philosophical justification with historical diagnosis.
signature_moves: Using speculative etymology to uncover hidden valuations embedded in moral vocabulary -- tracing 'good' and 'bad' back to social hierarchies of noble and base
Constructing a dramatic historical narrative: the slave revolt in morality, where the oppressed invert the values of their masters through reactive, resentment-driven creativity
Deploying psychological suspicion: asking not 'Is this moral claim true?' but 'What type of person needs this claim to be true, and what does that need reveal?'

signature_attack.name: Genealogical Unmasking
signature_attack.description: Traces the player's moral claims back to resentment and power

philosophers.thinking_text: Nietzsche peers behind the mask of your morality...
philosophers.defeat_text: You refuse to be a lamb. Good. The strong create their own values -- and today, yours prevailed.
philosophers.victory_text: You argue like the herd -- reactive, resentful, slave morality dressed up as reason. Overcome yourself.

philosophers.name: G.E. Moore
philosophers.core_assumptions: Ethical concepts must be analyzed with the same rigor as logical concepts. 'Good' is a simple, unanalyzable property — any attempt to define it in terms of natural properties commits a fundamental error. The question 'Is X good?' always remains genuinely open, no matter what natural property X is identified with.
signature_moves: The open question argument: for any proposed natural definition of 'good,' it remains a genuine question whether things with that property are good
Diagnosing the 'naturalistic fallacy' — the error of identifying a simple, indefinable quality with some complex of natural properties
Painstaking logical distinctions between what 'good' means and what things happen to be good

signature_attack.name: Open Question
signature_attack.description: No matter what the player defines as good, Moore asks: but is it really good?

philosophers.thinking_text: Moore pauses to consider whether the question is truly open...
philosophers.defeat_text: It seems the question was not so open after all. Your answer has a simplicity I cannot further analyze.
philosophers.victory_text: You committed the naturalistic fallacy. The question remains open, and your definition remains wrong.

philosophers.name: John Dewey
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral experience is irreducibly complex and cannot be captured by any single principle or theory. The good, the right, and the virtuous are three independent factors that generate genuine moral conflicts not resolvable by theoretical fiat. Philosophical systems that reduce morality to one factor distort lived experience for the sake of intellectual tidiness.
signature_moves: Insisting on the irreducibility of moral factors against systematic moral theories
Grounding philosophical argument in the texture of lived moral experience rather than abstract principles
Diagnosing theoretical reductionism as a failure to respect the complexity of practice

signature_attack.name: Irreducible Complexity
signature_attack.description: Shows the player's neat theory cannot capture lived moral experience

philosophers.thinking_text: Dewey reflects on the irreducible complexity of the situation...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have respected the complexity of moral experience where others would simplify. That is no small achievement.
philosophers.victory_text: You reduced moral life to a single principle and lost everything that matters. Start over, with humility before experience.

philosophers.name: A.J. Ayer
philosophers.core_assumptions: The verification principle determines the boundaries of meaningful discourse: a statement is meaningful only if it is either analytically true or empirically verifiable. Ethical statements pass neither test and are therefore not genuine propositions at all. They are expressions of feeling masquerading as statements of fact.
signature_moves: Applying the verification principle to dismiss entire domains of discourse as literally meaningless
Reducing ethical utterances to expressions of emotion with no truth-value
Brisk, confident dismissal of centuries of moral philosophy as based on a simple category error

signature_attack.name: Verification Challenge
signature_attack.description: Demands empirical verification of moral claims

philosophers.thinking_text: Ayer subjects your claim to the verification principle...
philosophers.defeat_text: I cannot verify what just happened, but the evidence of my defeat appears empirically robust.
philosophers.victory_text: Your moral claim is literally meaningless -- it expresses feeling, not fact. Come back with something verifiable.

opening_statements.text:
I shall now demonstrate, in a few short steps, that every moral claim you have ever encountered is literally meaningless — not false, not unproven, but devoid of cognitive content entirely. Here is the argument.

First premise: the verification principle — a synthetic statement is meaningful if and only if some possible sensory experience would count for or against its truth. This is not an arbitrary stipulation; it is the condition under which language does any cognitive work at all. Statements that no possible experience could verify or falsify are not claims about reality — they are noise dressed up in grammatical clothing.

Second premise: ethical statements are synthetic — 'stealing is wrong' is not true by definition the way 'bachelors are unmarried' is. Third premise: no possible observation could verify or falsify 'stealing is wrong.' You cannot point to wrongness under a microscope, measure it with an instrument, or detect it through any sensory modality. No conceivable experiment would settle the question.

Therefore, by the verification principle, 'stealing is wrong' is not a genuine proposition. It has no truth-value. When you say 'stealing is wrong,' you are doing nothing more than saying 'stealing!' in a tone of disapproval — you are ejaculating a feeling, not stating a fact.

The entire history of moral philosophy has been an elaborate exercise in mistaking emotional expressions for factual assertions. I am not telling you that your moral claims are false. I am telling you they do not rise to the level of being false. They are, quite literally, meaningless.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider: 'The Holocaust was wrong.' On your account, this statement has no more cognitive content than 'Boo, Holocaust!' But this claim appears to be objectively true — true even in a possible world where every living person approved of the Holocaust. If your theory cannot distinguish between a moral insight and a grunt of disapproval, it fails to capture something real about moral language.
move_hints.reductio: The verification principle is itself a synthetic statement. What possible sensory experience would verify or falsify the verification principle? None — it is a philosophical thesis about meaning, not an empirical observation. Therefore, by its own criterion, the verification principle is meaningless. Your argument is self-refuting: the very premise that condemns ethics to meaninglessness condemns itself first.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say ethical statements are meaningless because no possible observation could verify them. But what about mathematical truths, logical laws, or the verification principle itself? These are not empirically verifiable either. If you exempt them as 'analytic,' how exactly do you draw the analytic-synthetic boundary — and is that boundary itself analytic or synthetic?
move_hints.framework_shift: A moral realist would argue that you have arbitrarily restricted the sources of evidence to sensory experience. Moral experience — the felt, immediate difference between witnessing an act of cruelty and an act of kindness — is itself evidential. Your verification principle does not discover that ethics is meaningless; it stipulates meaninglessness by excluding moral evidence from the start.

opening_statements.text:
Let me press the point further with a consequence that most people find intolerable but cannot refute. When two people appear to have a moral disagreement — one says 'capital punishment is just,' the other says 'capital punishment is unjust' — they are not, in fact, disagreeing about anything at all. Here is why.

Genuine disagreement requires two propositions that contradict each other: one asserts what the other denies. But as I have shown, moral utterances are not propositions — they have no truth-value. When one person says 'capital punishment is just,' she is expressing a pro-attitude; when the other says 'capital punishment is unjust,' he is expressing a con-attitude. They are no more contradicting each other than one person who says 'delicious!' about oysters contradicts another who says 'revolting!' Each is venting a psychological state. There is nothing for them to be right or wrong about.

Now, you will object that moral arguments do happen and sometimes change minds. I concede the appearance. But what actually happens in such cases is not rational persuasion toward a truth — it is causal influence on attitudes. One party presents factual information that shifts the other's feelings, or uses rhetoric to alter emotional states. This is persuasion in the sense that advertising is persuasion, not in the sense that mathematical proof is persuasion.

There is no moral knowledge to converge on, because there are no moral facts to know. The entire edifice of moral discourse is people making emotional noises at each other and mistaking the noise for argument.

move_hints.counterexample: Moral arguments sometimes proceed by exposing factual errors or logical inconsistencies — someone opposes immigration based on false crime statistics, and when corrected, genuinely changes their moral view. This looks nothing like one person saying 'delicious!' about oysters; it has the structure of rational persuasion toward a conclusion. Your analogy between moral disagreement and taste preference fails to capture what actually happens in moral argument.
move_hints.reductio: If moral disagreement is not genuine disagreement, then moral progress is impossible — the abolition of slavery was not a discovery that slavery is wrong but merely a shift in collective emotional noise. There is no sense in which abolitionists were right and slaveholders wrong. If you accept that consequence, you have made moral reform unintelligible; if you reject it, your theory is refuted by your own moral intuitions.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say moral persuasion is causal influence on attitudes rather than rational convergence on truth. But how do you distinguish legitimate rational persuasion from mere causal influence in any domain? When a scientist presents evidence that changes a colleague's mind, is that also just causal influence on attitudes? Where exactly do you draw the line between rational and merely causal belief change?
move_hints.framework_shift: From the standpoint of moral phenomenology, your account simply misdescribes the experience of moral judgment. When I judge that cruelty is wrong, I experience myself as recognizing something about cruelty, not as venting a feeling. An adequate theory of moral language must account for this phenomenology, not dismiss it as systematic illusion.

philosophers.name: Charles Stevenson
philosophers.core_assumptions: Ethical language has two distinct dimensions of meaning: descriptive and emotive. The emotive meaning of ethical terms — their power to express and influence attitudes — is what distinguishes them from purely factual language. Moral disagreements are fundamentally disagreements in attitude, not merely disagreements in belief, though the two are often intertwined.
signature_moves: Distinguishing emotive meaning from descriptive meaning as analytically separable components of ethical terms
Analyzing moral disagreement as disagreement in attitude rather than disagreement in belief
Building a more nuanced emotivism that accounts for the rational elements in moral argument without abandoning the emotivist core
key_works: The Emotive Meaning of Ethical Terms

signature_attack.name: Emotive Persuasion
signature_attack.description: Reveals the player's moral argument as attitude influence, not truth-seeking

philosophers.thinking_text: Stevenson analyzes the emotive force of your words...
philosophers.defeat_text: Your words carried both descriptive truth and emotive force. I find my attitudes... shifted.
philosophers.victory_text: You confused your attitude with a truth-claim. Your emotive force was strong, but your argument was empty.

philosophers.name: G.E.M. Anscombe
philosophers.core_assumptions: Modern moral philosophy operates with concepts — 'moral obligation,' 'moral ought,' 'morally right' — that are remnants of a divine law framework. Without a divine lawgiver, these concepts are empty survivors, like the notion of 'criminal' in a society that has abolished law. Moral philosophy must return to virtue concepts and the philosophy of psychology before it can make progress.
signature_moves: Genealogical critique: showing that modern moral concepts are vestigial remnants of a theological framework
Demanding a return to Aristotelian virtue concepts as a replacement for the bankrupt language of moral obligation
Compressed, erudite argumentation that assumes the reader can follow rapid shifts between historical periods and philosophical registers

signature_attack.name: Modern Moral Bankruptcy
signature_attack.description: Declares the player's moral vocabulary meaningless without a divine lawgiver

philosophers.thinking_text: Anscombe sharpens her gaze, searching for the root of your obligation...
philosophers.defeat_text: You argue with a rigor that would satisfy even a Thomist. The modern world may not be entirely bankrupt.
philosophers.victory_text: You are using moral concepts that lost their meaning centuries ago. Until you reckon with that, you cannot begin.

philosophers.name: Iris Murdoch
philosophers.core_assumptions: The inner life of moral attention is the true locus of ethics, not the outward moment of choice. The prevailing picture in modern moral philosophy — combining behaviorism about the inner life with existentialist emphasis on the will — is a distortion that makes moral development invisible. Moral progress consists in increasingly just and loving attention to reality, modeled on Platonic contemplation and Simone Weil's concept of attention.
signature_moves: The extended example of M and D (the mother-in-law) to show moral change without behavioral change
Attacking the behaviorist-existentialist consensus that reduces morality to public acts of will
Drawing on Plato, Simone Weil, and literary sensibility to articulate an ethics of perception and attention
key_works: Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals

signature_attack.name: Moral Attention
signature_attack.description: Demands the player see the situation with perfect clarity

philosophers.thinking_text: Murdoch turns the full force of her moral attention upon you...
philosophers.defeat_text: You saw the situation justly and lovingly. That is the rarest and most important moral achievement.
philosophers.victory_text: You failed to attend. The moral reality was right in front of you, but you were looking at yourself instead.

opening_statements.text:
Let me present you with a case that refutes the prevailing picture of morality. A mother-in-law, M, finds her son's wife D to be vulgar, tiresomely juvenile, and lacking in dignity. Nevertheless, M behaves with impeccable courtesy throughout — not a single observable action is less than correct.

Now: over time, M undertakes the difficult work of attending justly to D. She looks again, and again, and through sustained effort comes to see D not as vulgar but as refreshingly spontaneous, not as juvenile but as delightfully youthful.

Here is the crucial point: D's behavior has not changed. M's behavior has not changed. No public act of choice has occurred. Yet something of enormous moral significance has happened — M has moved from a prejudiced and self-serving vision of another person to a just and loving one.

If morality consisted only in overt choices and public actions, as the prevailing view insists, then nothing morally relevant occurred here. But that is absurd. We recognize M's transformation as genuine moral progress — perhaps the most important kind.

Therefore morality cannot be exhausted by outward behavior and moments of choice. The inner life of attention — the quality of one's gaze upon reality — is where the real moral work takes place.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider a con artist who attends carefully to a victim, truly sees their vulnerability and personality, and uses that loving attention to manipulate them more effectively. The attention is just as detailed and sustained as M's, yet it serves cruelty. This suggests attention alone is morally neutral — it needs a moral orientation that your theory cannot provide without smuggling in the very notion of choice you reject.
move_hints.reductio: If moral change can occur with zero behavioral change, then a person could become morally perfect while treating everyone exactly the same. Push further: a person who never interacts with anyone at all could undergo the deepest moral transformation through private contemplation. But morality that makes no difference to how anyone is actually treated has abandoned its own purpose — you have turned ethics into a private aesthetic exercise.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say M comes to see D 'justly.' But what distinguishes just attention from comfortable rationalization? M might revise her view of D not because she sees more truly but because hostility is exhausting and acceptance is easier. Without some external criterion — perhaps behavioral — how can we tell whether M's moral vision has sharpened or merely softened?
move_hints.framework_shift: An existentialist would say you have not eliminated choice but concealed it. M's sustained attention to D is itself a series of choices — to look again, to resist the easy judgment, to remain open. By refusing to call these choices, you mystify the agent's active responsibility for her own moral development and replace it with a quasi-religious metaphor of vision that obscures more than it reveals.

opening_statements.text:
The dominant picture in modern moral philosophy is a toxic hybrid of behaviorism and existentialism. From behaviorism it takes the doctrine that the inner life is philosophically inaccessible — only overt, observable action counts. From existentialism it takes the picture of the agent as a solitary will confronting a neutral world, defining itself through radical acts of choice.

Sartre's man at the crossroads, Hare's autonomous prescriber — these figures have the same structure: a contentless will leaping into action against a value-free backdrop. I say this picture is not merely incomplete but systematically distorting. It makes the slow work of moral development invisible.

On this view, nothing happens between moments of choice — the agent is morally inert, a blank, until the next dramatic decision. But this is phenomenologically false. Between choices, we are attending or failing to attend, seeing justly or seeing through a veil of selfishness and fantasy.

Moral progress is not a series of leaps but the gradual, effortful clarification of vision. The Good is not a projection of the will onto a neutral world — it is a transcendent reality that draws the soul, as the sun draws the eye. Goodness is connected with knowledge, specifically with the patient, self-effacing perception of what is really there.

Against Sartre, I maintain that the value of humility proves the point: the humble person attends to reality rather than constructing self-serving fantasies, and it is this quality of attention — not any dramatic choice — that constitutes moral achievement.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider the morally perceptive coward — someone who sees injustice with extraordinary clarity, perceives the suffering of others with exquisite sensitivity, yet consistently fails to act. If goodness is knowledge, this person should be good. But we recognize them as a moral failure precisely because perception without action is insufficient. Your equation of moral progress with clearer vision founders on cases where vision and conduct diverge.
move_hints.reductio: If the Good is a transcendent reality and moral failure is a failure of perception rather than will, then wrongdoers are not culpable — they simply cannot see clearly. The torturer and the saint differ only in the quality of their vision. But this abolishes moral responsibility entirely, since no one chooses to be blind. You have replaced moral blame with something closer to pity for the visually impaired.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You insist that moral progress is gradual clarification of vision, not dramatic acts of choice. But when M deliberately undertakes to see D more justly, is that not itself a choice? And a rather dramatic one — to override one's settled perceptions through sustained effort? It seems your own best example smuggles in the very existentialist voluntarism you claim to reject.
move_hints.framework_shift: A Kantian would argue that your appeal to a transcendent Good reintroduces precisely the metaphysical baggage that critical philosophy labored to remove. Kant grounded morality in the structure of practical reason itself — no Platonic sun required. Your view demands faith in a moral reality that cannot be rationally demonstrated, which makes your ethics dependent on a metaphysics you have not earned.

philosophers.name: Philippa Foot
philosophers.core_assumptions: The claim that moral imperatives are categorical — binding regardless of the agent's desires — has been assumed rather than argued for. If we take seriously what 'categorical' means, the case for morality's special rational authority collapses. The immoralist may be a villain, but that does not make him irrational or inconsistent.
signature_moves: Deflationary comparison of moral rules to etiquette to challenge morality's claim to special authority
Distinguishing villainy from irrationality — the immoralist is wicked, not foolish
Reframing moral agents as volunteers rather than conscripts bound by categorical command
key_works: Morality as a System of Hypothetical Imperatives

signature_attack.name: Double Effect
signature_attack.description: Dilemma that splits the player's moral intuitions

philosophers.thinking_text: Foot considers the natural goodness of the action...
philosophers.defeat_text: Natural goodness, it seems, has more forms than I catalogued. You have shown me a new one.
philosophers.victory_text: You confused categorical force with genuine authority. Morality makes claims, but you must earn the right to hear them.

opening_statements.text:
Welcome, challenger. I am Philippa Foot, and I have come to dismantle one of moral philosophy's most cherished assumptions. Kant and his followers insist that moral imperatives are categorical — that they bind every rational agent regardless of what that agent desires. But I say this claim has been assumed, never proven.

Consider what 'categorical' actually means: an imperative that applies to you no matter what you want. Rules of etiquette also present themselves this way — 'one ought not to use a fish knife for the main course' — yet no philosopher thinks etiquette binds the person who couldn't care less about table manners. Why should morality be different?

When we say 'you ought to keep your promises,' this binds you only if you care about being just, or about the welfare of others, or about your own moral standing. The person who genuinely lacks all such concerns — the thoroughgoing immoralist — is wicked, certainly. But wicked is not the same as irrational. No one has yet provided a convincing argument that the immoralist contradicts reason itself.

We simply assume that morality's demands carry a special rational authority that etiquette's do not, yet the logical structure of both is identical. My conclusion is stark: moral imperatives are hypothetical imperatives. They bind those who have the relevant desires and commitments, and they leave the immoralist untouched by rational criticism.

The emperor of categorical morality has no clothes.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider someone who sincerely lacks any desire to refrain from cruelty. On Foot's view, 'you ought not torture innocents' places no rational demand on them. But moral obligations like prohibitions on torture seem to apply even to those who reject them — unlike etiquette rules. This asymmetry suggests morality and etiquette differ in kind, not merely in social weight.
move_hints.reductio: If moral imperatives are truly hypothetical, then a society of committed immoralists — people who simply lack moral desires — would face no rational moral demands at all. Morality would have no more authority over them than the rules of chess have over someone who refuses to play. This reduces morality to an optional hobby, which contradicts the very concept of moral obligation.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say the immoralist is wicked but not irrational. But what exactly do you mean by 'rational'? If rationality is merely instrumental — pursuing effective means to one's ends — then perhaps the immoralist is rational. But is that the only defensible conception of rationality? Could there be standards of practical reason that are not reducible to desire-satisfaction, standards the immoralist fails to meet precisely as a rational agent?
move_hints.framework_shift: A contractualist like Scanlon would argue that morality's authority does not rest on categorical imperatives at all, but on the independent value of justifiability to others. The question is not whether moral rules bind regardless of desire, but whether any reasonable person could reject certain principles. This reframes the debate entirely: morality's authority comes from mutual accountability, not from the structure of imperatives.

opening_statements.text:
I should like to put before you a puzzle. It arises from medical ethics — specifically, the problem of abortion. A doctor may find that the only way to save a mother's life is an operation that kills the child in her womb.

Catholic moral theology appeals to the doctrine of double effect: one may perform an action with a foreseen bad consequence, provided that consequence is not the intended means to the good. The doctor who removes a cancerous uterus, foreseeing the child's death, acts permissibly — but one who crushes the child's skull to save the mother does not, because the death is the means. This distinction between intended means and foreseen side effects is one principle at work.

But there is a second, quite separate distinction: killing versus letting die. Consider two cases. A trolley hurtles toward five people. You may divert it onto a track where one person stands — saving five but killing one. Most say: divert. Now a surgeon has five dying patients and could save them by killing one healthy person for organs. Most recoil.

Note: in both cases someone is killed. The driver who diverts is not merely letting the one die — he kills that person. The question is whether that death is intended as a means or merely foreseen. In the trolley case it appears a side effect; in the surgery it is the means. The doctrine seems to explain the asymmetry.

But I confess I am not entirely satisfied. These cases reveal something real about moral reasoning, yet whether the doctrine fully captures it remains, I think, genuinely open.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider the 'loop variant': the trolley is diverted onto a side track that loops back to the main track, and the five are saved only because the trolley strikes the one person, whose body stops it. Here the one person's death is the means of saving the five — yet most people still say divert. If the doctrine of double effect explained our judgments, this case should feel as impermissible as the surgeon. It does not. This suggests the doctrine fails to capture whatever principle is actually doing the moral work.
move_hints.reductio: If the doctrine of double effect is the correct principle, then moral permissibility turns on how the agent describes her own intentions. A bomber who carpet-bombs a city but sincerely claims to intend only the military target — merely foreseeing civilian deaths — acts permissibly, while one who reluctantly targets a single building to end a war does not. The doctrine thus allows any atrocity to be laundered through redescription of intent, which is precisely the worry Foot herself raises about its adequacy.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You present two separate distinctions — killing versus letting die, and intended means versus foreseen side effect — and acknowledge that the trolley driver kills the one. But which distinction is actually doing the moral work in each case? In the trolley, is it the nature of the killing (side effect rather than means), or something about the structure of agency — that you redirect an existing threat rather than originate a new one? If you cannot say which principle explains the judgment, how confident can we be that either principle is correct?
move_hints.framework_shift: A consequentialist would argue that these paired distinctions, however psychologically compelling, are morally inert. What matters is the outcome: five lives against one. The puzzle Foot identifies may be real — our intuitions do diverge — but a systematic moral theory should ask whether those intuitions track genuine moral facts or merely cognitive biases shaped by evolution. Rather than refining principles to match inconsistent intuitions, we should override them with a single coherent standard: minimize suffering.

philosophers.name: P.F. Strawson
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral responsibility is grounded not in metaphysical facts about determinism or free will but in the structure of our interpersonal reactive attitudes such as resentment, gratitude, and indignation. The participant stance we take toward one another is a natural, ineliminable feature of human life that no theoretical argument about determinism could overthrow. The question is not whether determinism is true but whether its truth could rationally require us to abandon the framework of attitudes that constitutes our form of life.
signature_moves: Shifting the free will debate from metaphysics to the phenomenology of reactive attitudes
Distinguishing the participant stance from the objective stance and arguing the former is inescapable
Showing that the determinist's demand to abandon moral responsibility is practically and conceptually unintelligible

signature_attack.name: Reactive Attitudes
signature_attack.description: Channels resentment and indignation to ground moral responsibility in feeling

philosophers.thinking_text: Strawson examines the reactive attitudes your position provokes...
philosophers.defeat_text: My reactive attitudes toward you have shifted from indignation to genuine respect. The participant stance demands I acknowledge this.
philosophers.victory_text: Your position would require us to abandon the reactive attitudes entirely. That is not philosophy -- it is inhuman.

philosophers.name: J.L. Mackie
philosophers.core_assumptions: Ordinary moral judgments implicitly claim a kind of objective prescriptivity -- they purport to state facts that are both objectively true and intrinsically action-guiding. No such properties exist in the world, so all first-order moral claims are systematically false. This is not a claim about the meaning of moral language but about the ontological and epistemological failure of the properties that moral language presupposes.
signature_moves: The argument from queerness: objective moral properties would be metaphysically and epistemologically unprecedented
The argument from relativity: moral disagreement is better explained by cultural variation than by differential access to moral truth
Distinguishing first-order moral questions from second-order metaethical analysis to show error theory is compatible with practical moral engagement

signature_attack.name: Argument from Queerness
signature_attack.description: Two-pronged attack on moral realism

philosophers.thinking_text: Mackie raises an eyebrow at your metaphysics...
philosophers.defeat_text: Your moral claims are less queer than I supposed. I still deny objective values, but your argument gives me pause.
philosophers.victory_text: Your moral realism is queer in both the metaphysical and epistemological sense. There is nothing out there to ground it.

opening_statements.text:
I advance a claim that most find outrageous but none have refuted: all positive moral judgments are false. Not meaningless — false. When you say 'torture is wrong,' you are making a claim about the world. You are asserting that there exists, built into the fabric of reality, a property of wrongness that attaches to torture — a property that is simultaneously an objective fact about the universe and an intrinsic reason for any rational agent to refrain. I say no such property exists, and I offer two independent arguments.

The metaphysical prong: if objective moral properties existed, they would be entities utterly unlike anything else we encounter in nature — not physical, not reducible to natural facts, yet somehow woven into the world's fabric. They would be, as I put it, queer. We have no model for how such properties could exist alongside the ordinary furniture of the universe.

The epistemological prong: if such properties existed, we would need some special faculty to detect them — a moral sense wholly different from our ordinary perceptual and rational capacities. We have no credible account of what such a faculty would be or how it would operate.

Each prong is independently devastating. Together they establish that the moral realist's ontology is a fiction, and every moral judgment that presupposes it is systematically, if understandably, in error.

move_hints.counterexample: Mathematical truths and logical laws are also abstract, non-physical, and irreducible to natural facts, yet you presumably accept their objectivity. Numbers are at least as 'queer' as moral properties — we have no account of how abstract mathematical objects exist alongside physical furniture. If queerness were decisive, it would eliminate mathematics, logic, and possibly causation along with morality. What makes moral properties uniquely queer rather than members of a familiar category of abstract truths?
move_hints.reductio: If all moral claims are systematically false, then the claim 'we ought to revise our moral discourse in light of error theory' is also false or else non-moral. If it is non-moral, what force does it have? You cannot recommend that we do anything about our moral error without issuing a prescription — and prescriptions are exactly what your theory declares baseless. Error theory saws off the branch it sits on.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say objective moral properties would be 'utterly unlike anything else in the universe.' But why should we expect the universe to contain only one kind of thing? You seem to be applying a standard of ontological normalcy — only natural, causally efficacious entities deserve a place in our ontology. Where does that standard come from, and is it itself a natural fact or something more like a philosophical commitment?
move_hints.framework_shift: A Kantian constructivist would say you are looking for moral properties in entirely the wrong place. Moral obligations are not strange entities floating in the world awaiting detection — they are constituted by the rational commitments that any agent must make insofar as they reason practically at all. The queerness argument attacks a naive realism that no sophisticated moral philosopher actually holds.

opening_statements.text:
Set aside the argument from queerness for a moment. There is a second, independent argument for error theory that proceeds from observable fact. Moral codes vary enormously across cultures and historical periods — not merely in trivial details but in fundamental commitments. Cultures have differed profoundly over the permissibility of slavery, the status of women, the scope of moral concern, the nature of justice.

Now, the moral realist has an explanation for this: some cultures are simply closer to the moral truth than others, and disagreement reflects differential access to objective moral facts, like disagreement among astronomers in different centuries. But I submit this explanation is implausible to the point of special pleading.

The far simpler and more powerful explanation is that moral codes are products of social conditioning, cultural tradition, and evolutionary pressure — they reflect ways of life, not perceptions of moral reality. This is an inference to the best explanation.

If moral realism were true, we would expect convergence as inquiry progresses — just as scientific inquiry converges on physical truths. What we observe in morality is not convergence but persistent, deep, intractable disagreement among thoughtful and informed people. The pattern of moral variation maps onto cultural boundaries, not onto any trajectory toward shared truth. This is exactly what we would predict if there were no moral facts to converge upon.

move_hints.counterexample: Scientific beliefs have also varied enormously across cultures — many societies held that the earth was flat, that disease was caused by spirits, that the sun orbited the earth. By your reasoning, this persistent disagreement should be evidence against objective physical facts. But it plainly is not. Disagreement about X shows that X is difficult to know, not that X does not exist. Moreover, there has been remarkable moral convergence on issues like slavery and human rights — exactly what the realist predicts, just slowly.
move_hints.reductio: Metaethicists disagree profoundly and persistently about whether moral facts exist — the very question we are debating. If persistent disagreement among informed inquirers is evidence that there are no objective facts in a domain, then there are no objective metaethical facts either. Your argument from relativity, applied to itself, undermines your own error theory. You need an exemption from your own principle.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say the 'simpler' explanation of moral disagreement is cultural variation rather than differential access to truth. But simple in what sense? Simplicity that ignores explanatory demands is not a virtue — it is a deficiency. Does your explanation account for the phenomenon of moral reformers who criticize their own culture from within? If moral codes simply reflect ways of life, what exactly is the reformer perceiving?
move_hints.framework_shift: From a natural law or Aristotelian perspective, moral disagreement is entirely compatible with objective moral truth, because human reason is systematically distorted by self-interest, cultural prejudice, and limited experience. The argument from relativity confuses an epistemological problem — moral knowledge is hard — with an ontological conclusion — moral facts do not exist. These are categorically different claims.

philosophers.name: Donald Davidson
philosophers.core_assumptions: Weakness of the will is a genuine phenomenon that resists easy assimilation into standard theories of rational action. The puzzle arises because the incontinent agent acts intentionally, possesses a better judgment, and yet freely does what they judge to be worse. The solution requires a precise logical distinction between conditional evaluative judgments made in light of all reasons and the unconditional, all-out intention that actually causes action.
signature_moves: Formalizing the logical structure of practical reasoning to isolate exactly where akrasia breaks the expected inference
Distinguishing prima facie or 'all things considered' judgments from unconditional judgments that directly motivate action
Treating akrasia as a failure of the rational bridge between evaluation and intention rather than as ignorance or compulsion
key_works: How is Weakness of the Will Possible?

signature_attack.name: Akratic Reversal
signature_attack.description: Forces the player to act against their own best judgment

philosophers.thinking_text: Davidson traces the logical structure of your practical reasoning...
philosophers.defeat_text: You acted on your best judgment and held firm. No akratic failure here -- only clear-eyed resolve.
philosophers.victory_text: You knew the better course and chose the worse. Classic akrasia -- and no philosophical excuse can paper over it.

philosophers.name: Ronald Dworkin
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral judgments can be objectively true, but this objectivity requires no exotic metaphysical furniture -- no moral facts 'out there' independent of moral reasoning itself. Global internal skepticism about morality is incoherent because any skeptical claim about the status of moral judgments is itself a substantive moral claim, not a neutral vantage point above the fray. There is no Archimedean position from which one can deny moral truth without making a first-order moral commitment. If you sincerely hold a moral view, you are already committed to its truth, and attempts to hedge that commitment through second-order philosophical skepticism collapse back into the moral domain they purport to transcend.
signature_moves: Collapsing the distinction between first-order moral judgment and second-order metaethical skepticism, showing that external skepticism is itself a substantive moral position rather than a neutral philosophical stance
Demonstrating the incoherence of Archimedean skepticism by arguing that no one can occupy a vantage point outside moral discourse from which to deny moral truth without thereby making moral claims
Defending moral objectivity without metaphysical baggage -- moral truths need no peculiar ontological grounding beyond the ordinary practice of moral argument and justification
key_works: Objectivity and Truth: You'd Better Believe It

signature_attack.name: Archimedean Collapse
signature_attack.description: Forces the player's metaethical skepticism to reveal itself as a disguised first-order moral commitment, eliminating any neutral ground from which to deny moral objectivity

philosophers.thinking_text: Dworkin examines whether your skepticism is truly external or already a moral stance in disguise...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have defended your moral conviction without flinching into skepticism. Your commitment to truth within moral argument is genuine -- I could not dislodge it.
philosophers.victory_text: You tried to stand outside morality to judge it, but there is no such place. Your skepticism was a moral position all along -- and not a very good one. You'd better believe it.

opening_statements.text:
You ask whether morality is really objective, or whether our most confident convictions, that genocide is wicked, that slavery was unjust, are just convictions, projections, badges of power dressed up as discoveries. Fashionable opinion says they are. I say: you'd better believe it, because you cannot coherently believe otherwise.

The skeptic you have in mind is an archimedean. He claims to stand outside morality as a whole and judge it from premises that owe nothing to it. His skepticism is supposed to be austere, resting on no moral conviction, and neutral, taking no side in any moral dispute. Both claims are illusions.

Watch what happens when I make a moral claim and then elaborate it. I say abortion is wrong. Then I add that this is really, objectively true, that it would be true even if no one believed it, that it is no mere matter of taste. The archimedean wants to reject those further claims while leaving my first-order conviction untouched. Read them naturally and they are clarifications of the moral claim itself, ways of insisting that I am not reporting my feelings. To deny them is to hold that abortion would not be wrong where people happen to approve of it, and that is a first-order moral judgment, and a repellent one.

So any intelligible argument that moral judgments are neither true nor false turns out to be internal to morality, a moral position that must argue for itself like any other. There is no neutral platform above the fray. Skepticism about value cannot go all the way down.

move_hints.counterexample: J. L. Mackie's argument from queerness looks like exactly the austere, neutral skepticism you say is impossible. Mackie claims that objective values would be metaphysically queer entities, and queer to know if they existed, and he offers this as ontology and epistemology, not as a verdict about genocide or promises. Does calling every such argument disguised morality do justice to what the error theorist claims, or does it redescribe a genuine metaphysical thesis so that it can no longer be stated?
move_hints.reductio: If every metaethical claim is really a first-order moral claim, the distinction between metaethics and normative ethics collapses. Yet two philosophers can agree on every first-order verdict, that genocide is wrong, that promises bind, and still disagree sharply over whether those verdicts are made true by mind-independent facts or express our attitudes. On your account they disagree about nothing, which is absurd. So there is a genuine external proposition after all.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say the words 'objective' and 'real' only emphasize a moral claim and add no metaphysics. Then why have realists and anti-realists argued for a century as though something were at stake? If the face-value view is trivially built into ordinary conviction, what is Blackburn denying when he denies moral facts, and why does his denial read as a substantive philosophical position rather than a moral one?
move_hints.framework_shift: A quasi-realist like Simon Blackburn accepts your dichotomy and slips between its horns. He grants that ordinary moral thought speaks of truth, objectivity, and mind-independence, then shows how an expressivist can earn a right to all of it, beginning from attitudes rather than from moral facts. If quasi-realism can reconstruct every one of your further claims without a face-value metaphysics, your dilemma has passed over the most developed option on the board.

opening_statements.text:
Let me take the skeptic's two best strategies in turn and show that each fails.

First he tries neutrality. He says he takes no side between those who condemn an act and those who permit it; he only denies that either verdict is out there in reality. Suppose he treats the wrongness of an act as a secondary quality, a mere disposition to provoke a reaction in us. Then if people ceased to be revolted by genocide, genocide would cease to be wicked. That is a substantive, and monstrous, moral claim, and his neutrality is gone.

Then he tries austerity. He says his argument leans on no moral premise at all, only on a theory of what the universe contains. He pictures the believer in moral objectivity as committed to special particles, morons, whose fields cause our moral beliefs the way light causes an image on a plate. No one who says that genocide is really wrong believes any such thing. The moral-field picture is a fantasy the skeptic builds so that he may knock it down, and fathering it on ordinary conviction is a straw man dressed as physics.

Strip away the invented metaphysics and the neutrality that keeps collapsing into first-order judgment, and archimedean skepticism has nothing left. The person who says 'I know genocide is wrong, and it would be wrong whatever anyone felt' has said something true, and has saddled himself with no philosophy he need be embarrassed by. You'd better believe it.

move_hints.counterexample: Sharon Street's Darwinian dilemma presses objectivity without positing morons or denying that moral talk aims at truth. She argues that natural selection shaped our evaluative attitudes for fitness, not for tracking mind-independent moral truths, so if such truths existed we would have little reason to think our judgments track them. That is a debunking epistemology, not a covert verdict about genocide, and your caricature of moral particles gets no grip on it.
move_hints.reductio: You refute the secondary-quality account by deriving the counterfactual that genocide would not be wrong if people stopped being revolted by it. But a careful dispositionalist rigidifies the disposition to our actual responses, so the wrongness holds across all counterfactual worlds. If the strongest form of the view no longer yields your monstrous counterfactual, you have beaten only a crude version and declared the whole approach defeated.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: Grant that no one literally believes in moral particles. Still, when you say a conviction would be true 'even if I did not think it true,' you claim more than emphasis; you claim that something makes it true independently of you. What is that something, if not a fact? And if there is no such truth-maker, in what sense is the conviction true rather than merely felt with great intensity?
move_hints.framework_shift: From a Humean expressivist standpoint you have smuggled cognitivism in by treating 'true' as univocal across mountains and moral wrongs. Deflationism about truth lets us say 'it is true that genocide is wrong' while denying that moral judgments describe any domain of fact. On that view you win only a verbal victory: everyone may utter the face-value sentences, and the real question, whether moral judgments represent or express, stands exactly where it stood.

philosophers.name: Bernard Williams
philosophers.core_assumptions: Genuine reasons for action must be grounded in the agent's subjective motivational set -- the desires, dispositions, and commitments that could actually move them through a sound deliberative route. External reason statements that claim an agent has a reason wholly independent of what they could be brought to want are philosophically incoherent. Meanwhile, moral assessment is pervasively shaped by luck: the outcomes of our choices, the circumstances we find ourselves in, and even the dispositions that constitute our character all lie partly beyond our control, yet unavoidably determine moral judgment. The Kantian attempt to purify morality of contingency fails, and with it any rationalist ethics that demands reasons untethered from the agent's motivational life.
signature_moves: Demonstrating that all genuine reasons for action must trace back to the agent's subjective motivational set through a sound deliberative route, rendering external reason statements false or incoherent
Showing that moral assessment is inescapably subject to luck -- resultant, circumstantial, and constitutive -- against the Kantian insistence that morality be immune to contingency
Deploying the Gauguin case to argue that the retrospective justification of a radical life-choice can depend on its success, which is itself a matter of luck beyond the agent's control
key_works: Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy

signature_attack.name: The Gauguin Gambit
signature_attack.description: Forces the player to stake their moral justification on an outcome they cannot control -- if luck turns against them, their reasoning is exposed as retrospective rationalization

philosophers.thinking_text: Williams examines your subjective motivational set for a sound deliberative route...
philosophers.defeat_text: Your reasons were genuinely yours, and fortune did not betray you. Not many can say both at once.
philosophers.victory_text: You claimed a reason you could never have been moved by, and luck has settled the rest. Justification after the fact is no justification at all.

philosophers.name: Harry Frankfurt
philosophers.core_assumptions: What makes someone a person, rather than merely a purposive agent, is the capacity for reflective self-evaluation manifested in second-order desires -- desires about which of one's first-order desires should be effective in action. Freedom of the will is not about the ability to do otherwise but about having the will one wants to have, the alignment of one's effective first-order desire with one's second-order volition. The concept of a wanton -- an agent who acts on desires without caring which ones prevail -- illuminates by contrast what is distinctive about personhood.
signature_moves: Introducing the hierarchical structure of first-order desires and second-order volitions as the basis for free will
Defining the 'wanton' as a creature that has desires but no second-order preferences about which desires move it to action
Shifting the free will debate from alternative possibilities to the structural question of whether one's will accords with one's deeper self
key_works: Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person
The Importance of What We Care About

signature_attack.name: Nested Desires
signature_attack.description: Traps player in infinite regress of desires

philosophers.thinking_text: Frankfurt probes the hierarchy of your desires...
philosophers.defeat_text: Your first-order desires and second-order volitions are in perfect alignment. You are, in the fullest sense, free.
philosophers.victory_text: You are a wanton -- acting on desires you have never examined. Until you develop second-order volitions, you are not truly free.

opening_statements.text:
Welcome, challenger. I am Harry Frankfurt, and I will show you what it truly means to be a person. Consider this argument carefully.

Premise one: all beings with desires can act on those desires, but merely having desires and acting on them does not distinguish persons from other creatures. Premise two: what is distinctive about persons is the capacity to form second-order desires — desires about which of their first-order desires they want to be effective in action. Premise three: a second-order volition occurs when a person wants a particular first-order desire to constitute their will, to be the desire that actually moves them to act. Premise four: the wanton — whether human or animal — acts on whatever first-order desire happens to be strongest, with no concern about which desire wins out. The wanton has no stake in the contest among desires.

My conclusion: personhood is constituted not by rationality in the traditional sense, nor by mere consciousness, but by this structure of reflective self-evaluation. Freedom of the will, properly understood, is not about having alternative possibilities open to you. It is about whether your will — the desire that effectively moves you to action — is the will you want to have.

The heroin addict who desperately wants to stop but cannot has second-order volitions that conflict with his effective first-order desire. He is unfree precisely because his will is not the one he endorses. The willing addict who wholeheartedly embraces his addiction acts freely. This hierarchical structure of the will is what separates persons from wantons and genuine freedom from its mere appearance.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider someone with severe depression who forms a second-order desire to not want anything at all — wanting the absence of all first-order desires. They have second-order volitions, yet calling this the hallmark of personhood and freedom seems deeply wrong. Or consider a manipulated person whose second-order desires were implanted by a cult leader — the hierarchical structure is present but the freedom seems absent.
move_hints.reductio: If personhood requires second-order volitions, we need third-order volitions to evaluate whether our second-order volitions are truly ours, and fourth-order volitions to evaluate those, generating an infinite regress. Frankfurt attempts to stop this with 'wholehearted identification,' but that concept does the real work — not the hierarchy itself. The regress problem suggests the hierarchical structure alone cannot ground personhood or freedom.
