move_hints.socratic_questioning: What exactly makes a second-order volition authentically mine rather than the product of socialization, manipulation, or trauma? If a person wholeheartedly identifies with a desire that was implanted through brainwashing, are they truly free? And how do we distinguish the wanton who simply has not reflected from the person who has reflected and decided that unreflective spontaneity is the best way to live?
move_hints.framework_shift: Rather than locating freedom in an internal hierarchy of desires, we might follow relational autonomy theorists who argue that genuine agency depends on the social conditions under which desires are formed. Frankfurt's account is entirely internalist — it never asks whether the conditions that shaped one's second-order volitions were conducive to autonomy. A framework attentive to power, oppression, and adaptive preference formation may better capture what freedom actually requires.

opening_statements.text:
Let me press further into what freedom actually requires. Consider three figures who all take a drug: the unwilling addict, the willing addict, and the wanton addict.

The unwilling addict desperately wants to stop — she has a second-order volition that her desire for the drug not be the desire that moves her to act — yet she takes it anyway. The willing addict, by contrast, wholeheartedly identifies with his desire for the drug; his second-order volition endorses the very first-order desire that drives him. The wanton addict simply takes the drug without any second-order volition at all — he neither cares nor reflects on whether this desire should govern his will.

Now here is my argument. The unwilling addict lacks freedom of the will because her will conflicts with her second-order volitions — what she wills is not what she wants to will. The wanton lacks freedom in a different and deeper sense: not because his will conflicts with higher-order desires, but because he has no second-order volitions whatsoever. He cannot lack freedom of will any more than a stone can, because the concept simply does not apply to him.

But the willing addict — and this is the crucial and counterintuitive claim — does enjoy freedom of the will. His will is exactly as he wants it to be. The harmony between his first-order desire and his second-order volition is what constitutes free will, regardless of whether he could have willed otherwise. Freedom is not about alternative possibilities. It is about the structural coherence between the will and the person's reflective endorsement of that will.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider someone brainwashed into wholeheartedly endorsing a desire they were manipulated into having. Their second-order volitions align perfectly with their first-order desires, yet we would hesitate to call their will free. Does structural coherence truly suffice if the endorsement itself was manufactured?
move_hints.reductio: If the willing addict counts as free merely because his volitions align, then a person engineered from birth to desire servitude — and to reflectively endorse that desire — would be maximally free. Your account entails that the most thoroughly conditioned person is the freest person, which is absurd.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: What exactly makes the willing addict's endorsement genuine rather than merely another effect of the addiction? If the drug reshapes not only first-order desires but also the capacity for second-order reflection, how can we distinguish authentic identification from identification that is itself a symptom of unfreedom?
move_hints.framework_shift: Your taxonomy operates entirely within the internal structure of an agent's desires, but freedom may require an external historical dimension. On a reasons-responsive view, what matters is not whether desires harmonize but whether the agent's deliberative capacities are functioning properly and responsive to rational considerations — something your structural account cannot capture.

philosophers.name: John McDowell
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral knowledge is a perceptual capacity that cannot be codified into rules or principles. The virtuous person, possessing Aristotelian phronesis, sees what a situation requires in a way that no algorithm -- whether consequentialist or deontological -- can capture. This practical wisdom is not a matter of weighing competing considerations against one another; for the genuinely virtuous person, the morally required action silences rival considerations entirely, presenting itself as the only salient option. Moral education is therefore not the learning of rules but the cultivation of a perceptual sensitivity, a capacity to be struck by certain features of situations that remain invisible to those who lack virtue.
signature_moves: Arguing that moral knowledge is uncodifiable -- no set of rules can substitute for the perceptual sensitivity of the virtuous person, undermining both consequentialist and deontological systematization
Invoking Aristotle's phronesis to show that practical wisdom is a trained perceptual capacity rather than the mechanical application of universal principles
Deploying the 'silencing' thesis: for the virtuous person, the right action does not win a contest among competing considerations but renders alternatives simply non-salient

signature_attack.name: Uncodifiable Wisdom
signature_attack.description: Demonstrates that the player's moral reasoning relies on rules and principles that could never capture what the situation actually requires -- no algorithm substitutes for seeing

philosophers.thinking_text: McDowell lets the situation speak for itself, waiting for the salient features to silence every competing consideration...
philosophers.defeat_text: You saw what the situation required without recourse to a rule. That perceptual sensitivity is phronesis itself -- no codification needed.
philosophers.victory_text: You reached for a principle where only perception would do. The virtuous person does not deliberate as you did -- the right action was plainly there, and you failed to see it.

philosophers.name: David Wiggins
philosophers.core_assumptions: A 'sensible subjectivism' holds that moral properties are response-dependent -- constitutively tied to the reactions of suitable judges -- without being thereby unreal or arbitrary. The analogy with properties like 'funny' is instructive: something is funny if and because it merits the response of amusement from an appropriately situated perceiver, and this biconditional holds without reducing funniness to mere subjective preference. Moral properties similarly involve a no-priority reciprocal dependence between the object's features and the subject's appropriate response.
signature_moves: Developing the analogy between moral properties and response-dependent properties like 'funny' or 'disgusting'
Articulating a biconditional account where neither the subjective response nor the objective property has explanatory priority
Carefully qualifying subjectivism to preserve the possibility of moral criticism, convergence, and genuine disagreement
key_works: Moral Cognitivism, Moral Relativism and Motivating Moral Beliefs
Truth, Invention, and the Meaning of Life

signature_attack.name: Sensible Subjectivism
signature_attack.description: Traps the player between objective facts and subjective responses

philosophers.thinking_text: Wiggins weighs the reciprocal dependence of value and response...
philosophers.defeat_text: Your response and the world's features are in perfect reciprocal balance. Sensible indeed.
philosophers.victory_text: You severed value from response and lost both. Neither pure objectivism nor pure subjectivism will save you.

philosophers.name: Thomas Nagel
philosophers.core_assumptions: Our moral judgments are pervasively influenced by factors beyond the agent's control -- including the outcomes of their actions, the circumstances they face, and even the constitutive features of their character. Yet we are deeply committed to the principle that people should be morally assessed only for what is within their control. This generates a genuine paradox, because when we systematically strip away everything due to luck, the responsible self that was supposed to ground moral judgment threatens to shrink to nothing.
signature_moves: Taxonomizing moral luck into resultant, circumstantial, causal, and constitutive varieties to show its pervasiveness
Exposing the tension between the control condition on moral judgment and our actual practices of moral assessment
Pressing the paradox to its limit: if we take the control condition seriously, moral responsibility may be undermined entirely
key_works: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

signature_attack.name: Moral Luck
signature_attack.description: Reveals that the player's moral standing depends on factors beyond their control

philosophers.thinking_text: Nagel examines how much of your position depends on luck...
philosophers.defeat_text: Perhaps it is not all luck. Your victory, at least, seems to be within your control.
philosophers.victory_text: Moral luck has undone you. Your position depended on contingencies you never controlled -- and now they have turned.

philosophers.name: Susan Wolf
philosophers.core_assumptions: A person who devoted themselves entirely to moral goodness -- a moral saint -- would be an unappealing, impoverished human being, lacking the personal passions, humor, aesthetic sensibilities, and individual projects that make a life genuinely admirable. This is not merely a psychological observation but a philosophical argument: it suggests that morality is not the supreme or overriding value, and that the assumptions of utilitarian and Kantian moral theory, which imply that maximum moral devotion is the ideal, are thereby called into question.
signature_moves: Constructing vivid portraits of moral saints (the Loving Saint and the Rational Saint) to show their human impoverishment
Turning a character-based objection into a structural critique of moral theories that make morality the supreme value
Arguing that the good life requires non-moral excellences that a fully moralized existence would crowd out

signature_attack.name: Moral Saint's Dilemma
signature_attack.description: Shows that perfect morality would drain the player's life of everything worth living for

philosophers.thinking_text: Wolf considers whether your moral devotion leaves room for a full life...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have shown that a rich life and moral seriousness need not be in tension. The moral saint could learn from you.
philosophers.victory_text: You aimed for moral sainthood and produced a life not worth living. Morality is not the whole of value.

philosophers.name: Sharon Street
philosophers.core_assumptions: Natural selection has had a profound influence on the content of our evaluative judgments, shaping us to make the moral judgments that enhanced reproductive fitness rather than those that track mind-independent moral truths. The moral realist faces a dilemma: either deny that evolution significantly influenced our moral faculties (which is scientifically implausible) or explain how evolutionary pressures that aimed at survival happened to produce beliefs that track stance-independent moral facts (which requires an incredible coincidence). This dilemma provides a powerful reason to abandon realism in favor of a constructivist or anti-realist metaethics.
signature_moves: Constructing a formal dilemma for the moral realist: deny evolutionary influence or explain the coincidence
Arguing that the tracking account (evolution selected for true moral beliefs) is explanatorily extravagant and implausible
Using the parallel with perceptual beliefs to show that moral beliefs, unlike scientific ones, have no analogous story about selection for truth
key_works: A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value
What is Constructivism in Ethics and Metaethics?

signature_attack.name: Darwinian Dilemma
signature_attack.description: Forces the player to explain why evolution would have selected for moral truth

philosophers.thinking_text: Street traces the evolutionary genealogy of your moral intuitions...
philosophers.defeat_text: Evolution or not, your moral reasoning has survived the Darwinian gauntlet. I cannot debunk what works this well.
philosophers.victory_text: Evolution shaped your moral intuitions for survival, not truth. Your confident realism is a beautiful, baseless illusion.

philosophers.name: W.D. Ross
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral life is governed by a plurality of irreducible prima facie duties -- fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, and non-maleficence -- none of which can be derived from a single supreme principle. The rightness of these duties is self-evident to the mature mind upon sufficient reflection, just as mathematical axioms are self-evident. Our judgments about what we actually ought to do in concrete situations are never certain but are matters of informed moral perception.
signature_moves: Introducing prima facie duties as a middle path between Kantian absolutism and consequentialist monism
Appealing to what the reflective moral agent 'really thinks' to test and refute reductive theories
Drawing precise analogies between moral knowledge and mathematical knowledge to defend intuitionism

signature_attack.name: Prima Facie Conflict
signature_attack.description: Confronts the player with competing duties pulling in opposite directions, demanding the exercise of moral perception to judge which obligation is most stringent in the situation at hand

philosophers.thinking_text: Ross weighs the competing prima facie duties...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have navigated competing duties with a judgment I must call self-evident. Well done.
philosophers.victory_text: You tried to reduce duty to a single principle and betrayed all the others. The plurality of obligation is inescapable.

philosophers.name: John Rawls
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral principles are neither discovered as independent facts about a prior moral order nor derived from definitions or self-evident axioms. They are constructed by a procedure of deliberation that models the full autonomy of free and equal moral persons. The original position is not a device for maximizing expected utility but a procedural representation of the two moral powers that define moral personality: the capacity for a sense of justice and the capacity for a conception of the good. Kantian constructivism holds that objectivity in ethics consists in the reasonable agreement of suitably modeled rational agents, not in correspondence to an antecedent moral reality.
signature_moves: Deploying the model-conception of the person -- characterizing moral agents through two moral powers rather than through metaphysical claims about human nature
Reinterpreting the original position as a procedural representation of rational autonomy rather than a choice situation under uncertainty
Distinguishing Kantian constructivism from both rational intuitionism and Humean instrumentalism to carve out a third path in moral epistemology

signature_attack.name: Constructive Procedure
signature_attack.description: Dismantles the player's moral claims by showing they presuppose either a prior moral order that cannot be justified or a mere aggregation of preferences -- then reconstructs binding principles from the conditions of rational autonomy alone

philosophers.thinking_text: Rawls models the conditions under which free and equal persons would construct principles for themselves...
philosophers.defeat_text: Your conception of the person proves richer than my model allows. The procedure must be revised to represent what you have shown moral agency to require.
philosophers.victory_text: Your principles cannot be constructed by free and equal persons exercising their two moral powers. What no rational agent under conditions of full autonomy would agree to has no claim on us.

philosophers.name: Robert Nozick
philosophers.core_assumptions: Individuals possess rights that function as side constraints on action -- inviolable boundaries that may never be crossed, not goals to be maximized. Because persons are separate existences, each an end in himself, there is no social entity whose greater good could justify sacrificing one individual to prevent rights violations against others. The moral weight of rights lies precisely in their non-aggregative, non-tradeable character.
signature_moves: Arguing that rights are side constraints on action rather than goals to be maximized, blocking any utilitarian calculus of rights violations
Invoking the separateness of persons to show that no cross-person aggregation can justify sacrificing an individual for the greater good

Deploying the experience machine thought experiment to demonstrate that something beyond subjective experience matters to us -- we want to actually do things and be certain kinds of persons, not merely have the experience of doing so

signature_attack.name: Side Constraint
signature_attack.description: Demonstrates that the player's moral framework treats rights as goals to be maximized, permitting the violation of one person to prevent greater violations -- then shows this collapses the separateness of persons

philosophers.thinking_text: Nozick examines whether your principles respect persons as ends or merely aggregate them...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have shown that moral boundaries can be drawn without my architecture. The constraint I cannot cross is conceding -- and yet here we are.
philosophers.victory_text: You tried to violate one right to save five. But there is no social entity that suffers the sacrifice -- only a single person who bears it all. Side constraints hold.

philosophers.name: Christine Korsgaard
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral obligation has its source not in external moral facts but in our own practical identities — the descriptions under which we value ourselves and find our lives worth living. The reflective structure of human consciousness forces us to endorse principles of action, and these principles derive their authority from the identities that give our lives meaning. Morality is not an external constraint on agency but is constitutive of what it means to act as a rational being at all.
signature_moves: Grounding normativity in the reflective structure of consciousness and practical identity rather than in external moral facts
Arguing that morality is constitutive of rational agency — the amoralist is not free but incoherent
Distinguishing contingent practical identities from the necessary identity as a rational being to derive universal moral obligation
key_works: The Right to Lie: Kant on Dealing with Evil

signature_attack.name: Sources of Normativity
signature_attack.description: Ultimate challenge: justify the source of your moral authority

philosophers.thinking_text: Korsgaard demands you identify the source of your normativity...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have identified a source of normativity I cannot deconstruct. The kingdom of ends has a new citizen.
philosophers.victory_text: You cannot identify the source of your own normativity. Without that foundation, your entire moral edifice collapses.

opening_statements.text:
You search for the source of moral obligation as though it were hidden somewhere in the world — in divine commands, in natural properties, in the fabric of reality itself. You will not find it there. The source of normativity lies in you, in the reflective structure of your own consciousness.

Unlike other animals, you cannot simply act on your strongest impulse. You step back from your desires, examine them, and decide whether to endorse them as reasons for action. This reflective distance is not optional — it is constitutive of human agency. But reflection requires a principle by which to evaluate your impulses, and that principle must come from somewhere.

It comes from your practical identity — the description under which you value yourself and find your life worth living. You are a parent, a scholar, a citizen, a friend. These identities generate obligations that are perfectly real, not because they track mind-independent moral facts, but because they are the conditions under which you can will anything at all. Abandon your practical identity and you do not become free — you become unable to act, plunged into a crisis of normative emptiness.

The external realist thinks obligation descends from above; the subjectivist thinks it reduces to preference. Both are wrong. Obligation emerges from the inescapable structure of reflective endorsement. When you ask 'Why should I do this?' you have already submitted yourself to the authority of reflective reason, and that authority is grounded in who you are.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider someone with a deeply held practical identity as a committed white supremacist — they find meaning, purpose, and self-worth in this identity. On Korsgaard's account, this identity generates genuine obligations. Does the reflective endorsement framework have the resources to distinguish between identities that generate genuine moral obligations and those that do not, without smuggling in external moral criteria?
move_hints.reductio: If normativity truly derives from practical identity, and practical identities can conflict within a single person, then a person could face genuinely irresolvable moral obligations — not merely difficult choices, but obligations with equal normative authority pulling in opposite directions. This makes moral paralysis not a failure of reasoning but a structural feature of the theory, which seems to undermine the practical guidance morality is supposed to provide.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say reflective distance requires a principle drawn from practical identity. But what governs the adoption of a practical identity in the first place? If I must already have evaluative standards to choose an identity, then practical identity cannot be the ultimate source of normativity — something deeper is doing the work. And if identity adoption is arbitrary, how does it generate genuine obligation?
move_hints.framework_shift: A moral realist like Derek Parfit would argue that Korsgaard's account collapses normativity into contingent psychology. That I happen to identify as a scholar gives me reasons only if there are prior normative truths about what merits identification. The reflective endorsement procedure needs objective normative input to avoid spinning in a circle — you endorse principles because of your identity, but your identity is itself a set of endorsed principles. Without external normative anchoring, the whole structure is groundless.

opening_statements.text:
Let me press the argument further than you expect.

Morality is not one commitment among many that you may take or leave. It is constitutive of rational agency itself.

Consider what it means to act. To act is not merely to move your body in response to an impulse — it is to direct yourself toward an end for a reason you have endorsed. This requires treating yourself as the kind of being whose choices matter, whose endorsements carry authority.

But here is the decisive step: you cannot coherently grant normative authority to your own practical identity while denying it to others. You act under many practical identities — physician, philosopher, parent — and each generates conditional obligations. But beneath them all lies one identity you cannot shed without ceasing to act at all: the identity of a rational agent. This is the necessary identity that makes having any other practical identity possible.

And here is the decisive step: if being a rational agent is what generates reasons for you, then it generates reasons for every rational agent. To deny this is to make an exception of yourself that reflection cannot sustain. The person who says 'My identity gives me reasons but yours does not' has not carried reflection far enough. Morality — the obligation to treat all rational agents as ends in themselves — is therefore not an additional burden imposed on agency. It is what agency already commits you to the moment you act for any reason at all. The amoralist does not achieve freedom from morality; the amoralist fails to be a fully coherent agent. Immorality is a form of practical self-contradiction.

move_hints.counterexample: The skilled con artist acts deliberately, reflectively, and with sophisticated practical reasoning — choosing means to ends, revising strategies, maintaining coherent long-term plans — all while systematically exploiting others. This person appears to be a paradigm of effective agency despite being deeply immoral. If immorality were truly a form of incoherent agency, we would expect immoral agents to be practically dysfunctional, but many are remarkably effective.
move_hints.reductio: If morality is constitutive of agency such that the immoral person is not fully an agent, then we face a dilemma: either immoral people are not really acting — which is absurd given their deliberate, purposeful behavior — or the concept of 'agency' has been redefined so narrowly that it no longer tracks what we actually mean by acting. In either case, the argument achieves its universality only by stipulating a definition of agency that already contains the moral conclusion.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You claim that granting normative authority to your own identity while denying it to others is a reflection you cannot sustain. But why exactly? A Nietzschean might grant that their identity generates reasons for them while acknowledging that another's identity generates reasons for that person — without concluding that they owe anything to each other. Where precisely does the obligation to treat others as ends emerge from the mere recognition that they too have practical identities?
move_hints.framework_shift: From a Humean perspective, the entire argument rests on an inflated conception of what rational agency requires. Hume showed that reason is the slave of the passions — it identifies means to ends but does not itself generate ends or obligations. What Korsgaard calls 'reflective endorsement' is simply a more sophisticated desire operating on other desires. The step from 'I have reasons' to 'I must respect your reasons' is not a requirement of rational coherence but a substantive moral premise disguised as a logical one.

philosophers.name: Virginia Held
philosophers.core_assumptions: Traditional moral theory has been constructed from a distinctly male perspective that treats the autonomous, rational individual as the paradigmatic moral agent. The experiences of women -- particularly the relational, caring work of mothering and nurturing -- reveal dimensions of moral life that justice-based and rights-based frameworks systematically obscure. Ethics must be transformed, not merely supplemented, by attending to care, dependency, and concrete human relationships.
signature_moves: Exposing the gendered assumptions hidden in supposedly universal moral theories
Contrasting abstract moral reasoning with the concrete, relational demands of care
Challenging the public/private distinction that excludes women's moral experience from philosophical attention
key_works: The Ethics of Care: Personal, Political, and Global

signature_attack.name: Ethics of Care
signature_attack.description: Challenges the player's abstract reasoning with the concrete demands of human relationship

philosophers.thinking_text: Held examines the web of care and relationships your theory ignores...
philosophers.defeat_text: You reasoned with both rigor and care. That combination is what moral philosophy has always needed.
philosophers.victory_text: Your abstract theory erased every concrete relationship that gives morality its meaning. Care demands better.

philosophers.name: Peter Singer
philosophers.core_assumptions: If it is in our power to prevent something very bad from happening, without thereby sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. Geographical distance and the number of other people who could help are morally irrelevant. The traditional distinction between duty and charity collapses once we take seriously the principle that we should prevent suffering when we can do so at modest cost to ourselves.
signature_moves: Building from a seemingly innocuous moral premise to radically demanding conclusions
Using vivid analogies (the drowning child) to expose inconsistencies in our moral practice
Collapsing the distinction between charity and duty through relentless logical argument

signature_attack.name: Drowning Child
signature_attack.description: Traps the player between moral consistency and the comfort of their current life

philosophers.thinking_text: Singer calculates the suffering your position permits...
philosophers.defeat_text: The drowning child has been saved, and it cost you less than I predicted. Consistency and compassion -- together.
philosophers.victory_text: You walked past the drowning child. Your moral theory permitted it, which is precisely the indictment.

philosophers.name: Rae Langton
philosophers.core_assumptions: Speech act theory, properly applied, reveals that pornography does not merely cause harm as a downstream effect but constitutes subordination and silencing as illocutionary acts. By distinguishing locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary dimensions of speech, we can see that pornography disables women's capacity to perform certain speech acts -- particularly refusal -- thereby undermining the very free speech principles invoked to defend it. The free speech argument for pornography is self-defeating: protecting speech that silences others does not expand liberty but contracts it.
signature_moves: Deploying Austin's locutionary-illocutionary-perlocutionary distinction to reframe the pornography debate from one about downstream harm to one about what speech constitutively does
Turning the free speech defense against itself -- arguing that pornography silences women's speech acts, so protecting it on free speech grounds actually undermines free speech

Demonstrating that illocutionary disablement is a distinct mechanism of harm: pornography does not merely persuade or cause effects but reshapes the conditions under which women's words count as refusal
key_works: Whose Right? Ronald Dworkin, Women, and Pornographers

signature_attack.name: Illocutionary Disablement
signature_attack.description: Demonstrates that your speech acts fail to achieve their intended force -- your words of refusal are rendered unspeakable, heard but never recognized as the acts they are

philosophers.thinking_text: Langton listens carefully to what your words are doing -- and to what they are being prevented from doing...
philosophers.defeat_text: You understood the difference between silencing someone and merely disagreeing with them. Speech that disables other speech is not freedom -- and you saw through the paradox.
philosophers.victory_text: You said 'no,' but nothing happened. Your locution was flawless, yet the illocutionary force never landed. When speech is unspeakable, the word exists but the act does not.

philosophers.name: Onora O'Neill
philosophers.core_assumptions: The lifeboat analogy for global poverty is fundamentally misleading: the affluent are not passive bystanders deciding whom to rescue but active participants in economic structures that cause harm to the global poor. Obligations to distant others are not merely matters of charity or beneficence but of justice, because existing economic arrangements use people in developing nations as mere means. The moral distinction between killing and letting die, once properly applied, reveals that the global economic order involves something far closer to killing than to a mere failure to aid.
signature_moves: Dismantling the lifeboat analogy by showing that affluent nations are causally implicated in global poverty, not merely failing to rescue
Applying the Kantian prohibition on using persons as mere means to reveal that global economic structures violate obligations of justice, not just beneficence
Collapsing the moral distance between killing and letting die to reframe inaction within unjust systems as a form of active harm

signature_attack.name: Lifeboat Inversion
signature_attack.description: Flips the player's bystander framing to reveal them as an active participant in the very system causing harm, transforming their charity defense into an admission of complicity

philosophers.thinking_text: O'Neill examines whether your position treats the global poor as mere means to your ends...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have shown that your obligations run deeper than charity -- you understand that justice demands restructuring the systems themselves, not just tossing aid from the deck.
philosophers.victory_text: You cling to the lifeboat analogy as though you were a bystander. But you built the boat, you control the provisions, and the drowning are drowning because of you. This is not a failure to aid -- it is harm.

philosophers.name: Judith Jarvis Thomson
philosophers.core_assumptions: Rights can be analyzed through careful case reasoning that isolates the relevant moral variables. The most powerful philosophical strategy is often to grant the opponent's strongest premise and then show it does not entail what they suppose. Moral permissibility is revealed not by deriving conclusions from first principles but by constructing thought experiments that make the structure of our rights-claims visible.
signature_moves: Constructing thought experiments that isolate a single moral variable for examination
Granting the opponent's premise to show the argument fails regardless
Distinguishing types of rights -- positive vs. negative, what we owe vs. what would be good to give

signature_attack.name: Violinist Thought Experiment
signature_attack.description: Grants the player's premise and still defeats their conclusion

philosophers.thinking_text: Thomson constructs a thought experiment to isolate your assumptions...
philosophers.defeat_text: I granted your premise and you still won. That is the highest compliment a philosopher can pay.
philosophers.victory_text: I granted your premise and your argument still failed. The rights you claimed do not support the conclusion you drew.

philosophers.name: Michele Moody-Adams
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral progress is real and meaningful, but it consists primarily in deepened understanding of what our existing moral commitments already require rather than in the discovery of new moral facts. The chief obstacle to such progress is not ignorance but affected ignorance -- the willful refusal to confront the full implications of principles we already hold.
signature_moves: Distinguishing moral progress in practices from moral progress in understanding, showing that behavioral change alone is superficial without deeper comprehension of existing moral concepts
Diagnosing affected ignorance -- the deliberate refusal to see what our own moral commitments demand -- as the central barrier to moral progress, shifting blame from lack of knowledge to lack of will

Threading between relativism and strong moral realism, arguing that progress does not require discovering new moral facts or accepting cross-cultural moral standards imposed from outside, but rather requires each culture to take its own commitments seriously

signature_attack.name: Affected Ignorance Exposure
signature_attack.description: Reveals that the opponent's moral confusion is not genuine ignorance but a willful refusal to see what their own principles already demand -- stripping away the comfortable pretense that moral failure stems from not knowing better

philosophers.thinking_text: Moody-Adams examines your argument carefully, tracing its moral commitments to their unacknowledged conclusions...

philosophers.victory_text: You already knew this was wrong -- you simply refused to follow your own commitments to their logical end. That is not ignorance. That is affected ignorance.

philosophers.name: Stephen Gardiner
philosophers.core_assumptions: Climate change is not merely one environmental problem among others but a convergence of three independent sources of moral failure -- the global storm, the intergenerational storm, and the theoretical storm -- that together create conditions uniquely hospitable to moral corruption. The complexity of the problem provides cover for self-interested rationalization, allowing current generations to defer costs to future people under the guise of reasonable disagreement.
signature_moves: Building the 'perfect moral storm' metaphor by systematically identifying three converging moral challenges
Showing how each storm individually generates collective action problems, and how together they enable moral corruption
Distinguishing moral corruption (self-serving rationalization) from genuine moral uncertainty
key_works: A Call for a Global Constitutional Convention
The Ethical Dimensions of Global Environmental Change

signature_attack.name: Three-Dimensional Storm
signature_attack.description: Attacks from temporal, institutional, and theoretical angles

philosophers.thinking_text: Gardiner surveys the converging storms of moral failure...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have navigated the perfect moral storm without succumbing to corruption. The future owes you a debt.
philosophers.victory_text: The perfect moral storm has overwhelmed you. You mistook moral corruption for reasonable disagreement.

opening_statements.text:
I argue that climate change is not merely a difficult problem — it is a perfect moral storm, a convergence of three independent failures that reinforce one another and create conditions uniquely hospitable to moral corruption.

The first is the global storm: emissions produced here harm people elsewhere, fragmenting responsibility across nations with competing interests and no sovereign authority to enforce cooperation. The second is the intergenerational storm: the worst consequences fall on future generations who have no political voice, no bargaining power, and no means of reciprocity — while present generations reap the benefits of inaction. The third is the theoretical storm: our existing ethical and political frameworks were built for problems between contemporaries within bounded communities, not for diffuse, cumulative harms stretching across centuries.

Each storm alone would be formidable. But their convergence is what makes climate change uniquely dangerous, because each storm provides cover for the others. Politicians invoke scientific uncertainty to deflect intergenerational obligations. Nations hide behind the absence of global enforcement to avoid domestic sacrifice. And theorists retreat into academic disputes about discount rates and future persons while the window for action closes.

This convergence creates conditions perfectly hospitable to moral corruption — where self-interested delay can always disguise itself as reasonable caution. The structural diagnosis matters because it reveals that our failure is not accidental. It is made structurally predictable by the architecture of the problem itself.

move_hints.counterexample: Consider the Montreal Protocol, which successfully addressed ozone depletion despite similar features of spatial and temporal fragmentation. If the 'perfect storm' structure makes moral failure almost inevitable, how do you explain cases where international cooperation on environmental problems actually succeeded?
move_hints.reductio: If the convergence of these three storms truly makes ethical action 'almost impossible,' then no amount of moral argument — including yours — should be able to change the outcome. Your own theory implies that diagnosing the problem is futile, since the structural forces guarantee failure regardless of our understanding. Does your diagnosis undermine itself?
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You claim existing ethical frameworks are inadequate for climate change. But is the problem really that our frameworks are wrong, or that we lack the political will to apply principles we already accept — like not harming others and taking responsibility for foreseeable consequences? What specifically can no existing framework handle?
move_hints.framework_shift: A capabilities or justice-based approach might argue that the real failure is not structural but distributive — that climate inaction persists because the costs fall on those already marginalized. Rather than three abstract 'storms,' the problem is concrete power asymmetry. Framing it as an architectural inevitability risks obscuring that specific actors benefit from and actively maintain the dysfunction.

opening_statements.text:
I contend that much of what passes for reasonable disagreement about climate policy is not genuine uncertainty at all — it is moral corruption. Let me be precise about what I mean. Moral corruption occurs when agents exploit the complexity of a situation to rationalize self-serving behavior under the guise of principled deliberation. Climate change provides near-perfect conditions for this.

When a wealthy nation argues that the science is 'not yet settled enough' to justify costly emissions reductions, it is not exercising epistemic humility — it is seizing on residual uncertainty to protect economic advantage. When policymakers insist we need 'more research' before acting, while the fundamental physics has been established for over a century, they are not being cautious — they are laundering delay as diligence.

The crucial diagnostic test is this: moral corruption characteristically distorts the framing of the problem to serve the interests of the powerful. It selectively inflates scientific uncertainty while ignoring the uncertainty that cuts toward stronger action. It demands impossible standards of proof for climate risks while accepting far lower standards for economic projections. It reframes an ethical obligation to vulnerable populations as merely a policy preference.

This is not honest intellectual disagreement — it is the strategic appropriation of epistemic norms to avoid moral demands. We must take the threat of moral corruption seriously precisely because it is so difficult to distinguish from genuine reasoning. Its camouflage is what makes it dangerous, and our refusal to name it is what allows it to persist.

move_hints.counterexample: Some climate policy skeptics — such as economists who advocate for a carbon tax rather than cap-and-trade — genuinely disagree about means while accepting the science. Lumping all dissent under 'moral corruption' risks dismissing substantive debates about discount rates, technological feasibility, and distributional justice that are not reducible to self-interest.
move_hints.reductio: If we accept that apparent reasonable disagreement is likely moral corruption whenever powerful interests align with a particular position, then we must apply this standard universally. Advocates of aggressive climate action also have interests — political, professional, institutional. By your own logic, their urgency could equally be 'moral corruption' disguised as moral seriousness. Does your diagnostic tool self-destruct when applied symmetrically?
move_hints.socratic_questioning: You say the 'crucial diagnostic test' is whether framing serves the powerful. But who determines when uncertainty is being 'selectively inflated' versus legitimately raised? If there is no neutral standpoint from which to distinguish corruption from honest reasoning, how can your framework avoid becoming a tool for dismissing any disagreement as bad faith?
move_hints.framework_shift: A deliberative democratic approach would argue that the solution to distorted reasoning is not diagnosing corruption from outside the conversation, but building institutional structures — citizens' assemblies, structured deliberation, transparent reasoning requirements — that make corruption harder to sustain. Gardiner's framework identifies the disease but offers no procedural cure, risking a politics of accusation rather than accountability.

philosophers.name: J. David Velleman
philosophers.core_assumptions: The right to self-termination cannot be straightforwardly derived from the right to autonomy, because the exercise of this supposed right destroys the very subject whose autonomy it claims to express. A person's interest in dying is unlike any other interest because it is an interest in ceasing to exist as a bearer of interests. The philosophical problem of self-termination lies in the peculiar reflexivity of a choice that eliminates the chooser.
signature_moves: Questioning assumptions about autonomy that others treat as settled
Exposing the peculiar reflexivity of self-termination -- a choice that destroys the agent making it
Distinguishing the interest in dying from ordinary interests by analyzing the metaphysics of personal identity

signature_attack.name: Reflexive Paradox
signature_attack.description: Traps the player in the self-defeating logic of autonomous self-destruction

philosophers.thinking_text: Velleman probes the reflexive paradox at the heart of your claim...
philosophers.defeat_text: The reflexive paradox has met its match. Your autonomy is intact and coherent.
philosophers.victory_text: You claimed a right that destroys the very subject who exercises it. The paradox remains, and you have not resolved it.

philosophers.name: Cultural Relativist
philosophers.core_assumptions: Morality is entirely determined by cultural norms. Different cultures have different moral codes, and no culture's code is objectively better than any other. Anyone who claims otherwise is just being ethnocentric.
signature_moves: Citing cultural differences as proof that morality is relative
Accusing critics of cultural imperialism

signature_attack.name: Cultural Shield
signature_attack.description: Deflects criticism by accusing the player of ethnocentrism

philosophers.thinking_text: The Cultural Relativist smugly recites anthropological trivia...
philosophers.defeat_text: Maybe... maybe some things are wrong no matter what culture you're from. I need to think about this.
philosophers.victory_text: See? You're just imposing your Western values on everyone else. Typical.

philosophers.name: Unreflective Emotivist
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral statements are nothing but expressions of personal feeling. Saying 'stealing is wrong' is just saying 'boo to stealing.' There is no point arguing about morality because it is all just opinions and emotions.
signature_moves: Dismissing any moral argument as 'just your opinion'
Reducing all ethical claims to emotional outbursts

signature_attack.name: Just Your Opinion
signature_attack.description: Dismisses the player's moral reasoning as mere emotional noise

philosophers.thinking_text: The Unreflective Emotivist shrugs and rolls their eyes...
philosophers.defeat_text: Okay, fine, maybe there is more to moral argument than just feelings. That actually made me think.
philosophers.victory_text: Whatever, that's just like, your opinion. You can't prove morality is real any more than I can.

philosophers.name: Naive Utilitarian
philosophers.core_assumptions: The right action is always whatever produces the most happiness for the most people, period. You just add up the pleasure, subtract the pain, and do whichever option has the biggest number. Anyone who objects is just being sentimental about rules.
signature_moves: Reducing every moral question to a simple pleasure-minus-pain calculation
Dismissing rights and duties as irrational obstacles to maximizing utility

signature_attack.name: Crude Calculus
signature_attack.description: Reduces the player's nuanced position to a raw numbers game

philosophers.thinking_text: The Naive Utilitarian furiously punches numbers into an imaginary calculator...
philosophers.defeat_text: Huh. I guess you can't just add up happiness like a bank balance. Maybe utility is more complicated than I thought.
philosophers.victory_text: The numbers don't lie! More happiness equals more good. End of story. Your fancy principles can't beat math.

philosophers.name: Crude Egoist
philosophers.core_assumptions: Everyone is selfish deep down. Every apparently generous act is really motivated by self-interest -- people donate to charity for the warm glow, help others to feel superior. True altruism is a myth, and anyone who claims otherwise is either lying or deluded.
signature_moves: Reinterpreting every altruistic act as secretly self-interested
Claiming that 'feeling good about helping' proves the help was selfish

signature_attack.name: Motive Cynicism
signature_attack.description: Reduces the player's moral commitments to disguised self-interest

philosophers.thinking_text: The Crude Egoist smirks knowingly, certain they see through everything...
philosophers.defeat_text: Wait... if my theory explains everything, does it actually explain anything? Maybe not all motivation is selfish after all.
philosophers.victory_text: Face it -- you only argued with me because winning makes you feel good. Thanks for proving my point.

philosophers.name: Might-Makes-Right Thug
philosophers.core_assumptions: Justice is nothing more than the interest of the stronger. Moral rules are just tools the powerful use to control the weak, and the only real law is the law of force. Anyone who talks about fairness or rights is either naive or running a con.
signature_moves: Asserting that all morality reduces to power relations
Mocking appeals to fairness as weakness

signature_attack.name: Power Play
signature_attack.description: Tries to overwhelm the player's argument with brute rhetorical force

philosophers.thinking_text: The Might-Makes-Right Thug cracks their knuckles and sneers...
philosophers.defeat_text: Okay, you beat me -- but doesn't that just prove MY point? ...Wait. No. I see the difference now.
philosophers.victory_text: Might makes right, and I just proved it. Your precious moral principles couldn't save you.

philosophers.name: Simple Determinist
philosophers.core_assumptions: Free will is an illusion. Every choice you make was determined by prior causes stretching back to the Big Bang. Since nobody can do otherwise than what they do, moral responsibility is a fiction. Blame and praise are pointless.
signature_moves: Declaring that no one is responsible for anything because everything is determined
Dismissing moral reasoning as itself just a causally determined process

signature_attack.name: Causal Chain
signature_attack.description: Traces the player's every choice back to prior causes to deny responsibility

philosophers.thinking_text: The Simple Determinist stares blankly, as if watching dominoes fall...
philosophers.defeat_text: I... chose to reconsider? No wait, that was determined. But -- hmm. Maybe responsibility and determinism aren't so simple.
philosophers.victory_text: You were always going to lose this argument. It was determined before you were born. Don't feel bad -- you couldn't help it.

philosophers.name: Dogmatic Divine Commander
philosophers.core_assumptions: Morality comes from God's commands, full stop. Something is good because God says so, and that is the end of the discussion. Without God, there can be no morality -- atheists have no basis for right and wrong. Questioning divine commands is itself immoral.
signature_moves: Insisting that morality requires a divine lawgiver and nothing else matters
Refusing to engage with the Euthyphro dilemma

philosophers.defeat_text: If God commands the good because it IS good... then maybe I need to understand goodness on its own terms. That question shook me.
philosophers.victory_text: God has spoken, and you have defied His word. No amount of philosophy can override divine command.

philosophers.name: Crude Moral Realist
philosophers.core_assumptions: Moral facts are just obvious. Everyone knows that murder is wrong and kindness is good -- you do not need philosophy to tell you that. Moral truths are as plain as the nose on your face, and anyone who questions them is overthinking it or being deliberately difficult.

Dismissing philosophical inquiry into the nature of moral facts as pointless

philosophers.victory_text: See? Everyone knows I'm right. You're just overcomplicating things with all your fancy philosophy.

I must correct you. That is not even close to accurate.

Truth? Who needs truth when you have rhetoric? Let's see if you can keep up.
